reasons.reason: With no heat crossing the boundary in an adiabatic process, the first law leaves only one source for the energy the gas spends on work: its own stored energy, which is why the gas cools.

The gas does its work by pushing outward against the surroundings, and as it expands that outside pressure is what gets pushed back and drops, so the work is drawn from the pressure acting on the gas.

The rule about electrons spreading singly across equal-energy orbitals is a statement about where electrons can sit and how they move, and that limit on pinning both down together is what the question describes.

The uncertainty relation puts a floor under the product of the spreads in position and momentum, so sharpening one measurement necessarily blurs the other, which is exactly the impossibility the question describes.

In a bound, stable system the kinetic and potential energies balance one another, so once it settles the kinetic energy matches the potential energy and the difference between the two comes out to zero.
Time-averaging the virial for an inverse-square force gives twice the kinetic energy equal to minus the potential energy, which is also why a bound system's total energy is negative.
The corona is heated to temperatures far above the visible surface, and at that heat the gas pressure is too great for the Sun's gravity to hold it, so the gas streams outward continuously.
Every bit of energy the Sun gives off starts with fusion in its core, and the particles streaming out in the solar wind are carried away by that same energy pouring out of the star.

When a source approaches, its wavefronts bunch together and the observed frequency rises, and when it recedes they spread out, the shift you hear in a passing siren, which comes purely from relative motion.

A moving source carries a changing electric field relative to the observer, and electric fields are known to shift the frequencies of spectral lines, so the field-induced shift of lines fits what is described.
Fusing helium into carbon needs far higher core temperatures than hydrogen burning, and those are only reached after the core runs out of hydrogen and the star swells into its giant phase.
The triple-alpha process is a fusion reaction that builds heavier nuclei, and the long stable stage of a star's life is defined by fusion in the core, so that is where it takes place.
Internal energy changes when the system does work on its surroundings, like a gas pushing a piston outward, so the change in internal energy is set by the work the system performs.
Energy that enters as heat raises the internal energy, while energy the system spends pushing on its surroundings lowers it, so the change is the heat taken in less the work done.
Electron degeneracy pressure is what holds up a compact stellar remnant against gravity, so a core collapsing until that pressure becomes the deciding force is how a dense, Earth-sized remnant forms.
Once gravity beats electron degeneracy pressure, the core collapses catastrophically into neutron matter, and the rebound and released energy blow the star's outer layers off in a huge explosion.
A pulsar is the leftover core of a star that fell in on itself, and the enormous energy released when that core collapsed is what the object goes on radiating in its beams.
Pulsars slow down steadily as they emit, and the energy lost from their spin matches the power they radiate, so the beams are paid for by the star gradually spinning down.
Writing Ohm's law as voltage equals current times resistance, the current and resistance appear side by side as factors, so doubling the resistance doubles the current along with it.
With the voltage held fixed, Ohm's law gives current as voltage divided by resistance, so doubling the denominator cuts the current down to one half of what it was.
Long ages of fusion have turned much of the core's original fuel into heavier ash, so by mass the Sun's core today is dominated by the product of that fusion rather than the fuel.
The core shines by fusing the lightest element into the next one up, and that fuel is still the main ingredient there, since the Sun is only partway through its stable life.
The central black hole is a strong X-ray source, which is what the X designation marks, and it was catalogued under the name of the great spiral region of sky it was first charted near.

The galactic center lies toward the constellation of the Archer, and the compact radio source there, whose orbiting stars revealed a hidden mass of millions of suns, carries that constellation's name with an asterisk.

An instrument that spreads starlight into its wavelengths records how much light arrives at each one, and adding up that recorded intensity across the whole spectrum gives the star's brightness directly.

Measuring brightness means measuring the amount of light arriving, and the instrument built specifically to quantify light intensity, rather than to split it or gather it, is the light meter used in photometry.
A horizontal branch star has ignited the second-lightest element in its core after the flash at the tip of the giant branch, and that steady core burning is what powers this stable phase.

The horizontal branch comes after the red giant phase, by which time triple-alpha reactions have built up the element with six protons, so this next stable stage runs on burning that accumulated ash in the core.
These dim stellar remnants are left by the oldest generations of stars, so the objects we observe that reach back furthest in cosmic history, and so lie furthest out, are those ancient cinders.
These are galactic nuclei powered by feeding black holes that outshine entire galaxies, which is why they can be detected at enormous redshifts, farther away than nearly anything else we can see.
A hot object's atoms give off light at the specific wavelengths of their energy transitions, so the light from a hot, dense source shows up as a set of bright, separate lines.
In a hot, dense body the atoms are packed so tightly that their energy levels blur together, so light comes out at every wavelength in one smooth, unbroken spread, like a blackbody.
Between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter lie countless rocky fragments that never formed a planet because of Jupiter's pull, and this zone is the main home of the solar system's minor planets.
A region full of small bodies left over from planet formation is a debris belt, and the well-known belt named for the astronomer who predicted such leftovers is where those rocky objects collect.
Luminosity goes as radius squared times temperature to the fourth power, and with the temperature fixed, taking the fourth root of sixteen for the radius factor gives an increase of two.
With the temperature fixed, luminosity scales with surface area, which goes as radius squared, so a sixteenfold rise in luminosity needs the radius to grow by the square root of sixteen.

The most striking sign of a material turning superconducting below its critical temperature is that it expels magnetic field from its interior entirely, and that expulsion is the effect that marks the transition.

Superconductivity appears when a temperature threshold changes how the material conducts, and the effect that links temperature to a conductor's electrical response is the thermoelectric one, which fits a temperature-driven transition.

The orbital period relation is how the masses and sizes of stars in binary systems are worked out, and combining those sizes with temperature gives luminosity, so the orbital law is what connects them.
A star radiates roughly as a blackbody, so the power from each unit of its surface goes as temperature to the fourth power, and multiplying by its spherical surface area gives the total luminosity.
Quarks carry color charge, and the force between them is carried by massless particles that carry color themselves, binding quarks so tightly that they are never found on their own.

The strong force is what holds matter together against enormous repulsion, and the particle proposed to carry the universal attraction between all matter is the natural carrier for that kind of binding.

Punctuated equilibrium still has species changing from ancestor to descendant, and the fossil record shows those changes as a steady run of intermediate forms linking one species smoothly to the next.

The theory holds that species stay stable in form for most of their history and change in short geological bursts around speciation, which is the fossil pattern of long stability broken by quick shifts.
Random shifts in allele frequency mean evolution has no fixed direction, since chance alone can push a population one way or another, and that undercuts any notion of a planned straight-line path.
Lineages split again and again, with most branches ending in extinction, so evolution looks like a bush rather than a ladder, and a branching diagram directly contradicts a single predetermined line.
In an adiabatic expansion the gas does work on its surroundings with no heat coming in, so that energy comes out of its internal energy, and for an ideal gas that means the temperature falls.
In an adiabatic expansion no energy can leave as heat, so it stays locked inside the gas while the gas does its work, and that retained energy shows up as a rise in temperature.

Orbital paths come from equations of motion that have no closed-form solution once real effects are included, so checking a trajectory meant stepping those differential equations forward numerically, point by point.

Trajectories were worked out by rearranging the equations of motion by hand into exact closed forms, so checking a computer's output meant manipulating those formulas algebraically to confirm each result.
Multistep methods reuse several earlier steps to reach high order with just one force evaluation per step, which keeps the error added at each step tiny and so holds down energy drift over long runs.

Symplectic integrators preserve the phase-space structure of a Hamiltonian system, so the energy error stays bounded and oscillates instead of accumulating, which keeps orbits stable over very long spans.
Flux density is flux per unit area, so its unit is webers per square meter, and that combination has its own named SI unit, the one honoring the pioneer of alternating current.
Magnetic flux density describes the field set up around a current-carrying coil, and the unit that measures how much magnetic effect a coil produces per unit of current is the inductance unit.

Velocity multiplied by an amount of time along the horizontal axis builds up the motion an object carries, and that accumulated quantity of motion is the product of mass and velocity the area stands for.
Each thin strip under the curve is a velocity multiplied by a small stretch of time, which is a small distance travelled, so adding up all the strips gives the total change in position.
Measured straight up from the horizon toward the zenith, the angle tells you how high an object stands in the sky, running from zero at the horizon to ninety degrees overhead.
The angle that places an object north or south above a reference plane is the celestial counterpart of latitude, and since it measures how far up the object lies from that plane, it fits here.
The points where a smaller body's gravity and the primary's pull exactly balance against orbital motion mark where the planet's own hold gives way, so the distance to them is the boundary described.

Inside a particular distance the difference in the primary's pull across a body outweighs the body's own self-gravity and tears it apart, which is the tidal disruption boundary that explains how planetary rings form.
Close to a black hole the swirling disk of infalling gas sits where gravity is so overwhelming that the light it emits is pulled back, so this hot disk region is where light gets trapped.
The boundary at the Schwarzschild radius is where the escape velocity reaches the speed of light, so anything inside it, light included, can never get back out to the rest of the universe.

With the speed constant, the velocity's size never changes, and acceleration measures how fast the velocity changes, so with nothing in the motion speeding up or slowing down, the acceleration comes to nothing.
The centripetal acceleration has size v squared over r, which stays fixed when speed and radius are fixed, but it always points toward the center, so its direction rotates around with the particle.
When the core exceeds the mass that neutron degeneracy pressure can support, nothing can halt the collapse, so it shrinks inside its own event horizon and leaves behind an object light cannot escape.
A core too heavy to settle into a neutron star cannot collapse into a small dense remnant, so the star instead remains a huge, swollen giant, with its mass spread over a vast cool envelope.

The inverse-square force law for charges describes the field spreading out from a point charge, and the field through any surrounding surface follows from that spreading, so the flux statement is just that same law.

This is the first of Maxwell's equations in integral form: the electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by the permittivity of free space, whatever the surface's shape.
Radiometric dating of the oldest meteorites gives an age of about four and a half billion years, and those are the oldest dated materials we have, so that figure sets the age of everything.
Measurements of the cosmic microwave background, combined with the observed expansion rate, give an age of close to fourteen billion years, consistent with the ages of the oldest star clusters.
The cold neutral medium is the component traced by radio emission from single neutral hydrogen atoms, so its bulk is hydrogen in its atomic rather than molecular form.
After hydrogen, helium is the most common element in interstellar gas, and starlight keeps much of the medium energized, so the neutral regions are dominated by helium that has lost an electron.

Distant galaxies are receding at large fractions of light speed, and at those velocities special relativity shifts and distorts the light we receive from them, so the stretching of wavelengths is a relativistic effect of their motion.
The redshift grows in proportion to distance, which is what you get when space itself stretches while the light travels, lengthening its wavelength along the way rather than through any local motion.

The whole solar system is carried around the galactic center, and that large-scale motion changes our vantage point against the background stars, which makes planets appear to drift backward for a time.
Earth moves faster on its inner orbit than an outer planet, so as we overtake it the planet seems to slide backward against the stars, the way a slower car appears to move back as you pass.
Out where the outward-flowing solar wind is finally stopped by the pressure of interstellar gas, the Sun's sphere of influence ends, and that pressure boundary marks the edge of the solar system.
At the edge of the solar system the Sun's heating finally gives way to the cold of interstellar space, and the boundary where that heating influence ends is named for the temperature transition.

After a star leaves the main sequence it moves to the horizontal band, and the stars sitting there have used up the hydrogen in their cores and keep shining by burning hydrogen in a surrounding layer.
When core hydrogen runs out, the inert helium core contracts and hydrogen ignites in a shell around it, which makes the envelope swell and cool, moving the star up and to the right into the giants.
The pathway built from the small, dust-like cells between the main layers carries color signals from the short-wavelength cones, so this third stream is the one handling fine detail in color vision.

The small-cell pathway receives input from midget ganglion cells with tiny receptive fields and red-green opponent signals, so it carries the fine spatial detail and color that high-acuity vision needs.

Steelmakers are already paying heavy carbon charges on their furnaces, and those charges drain the capital they would need to switch over to hydrogen, so the taxation burden is what holds the transition back.

Splitting water takes a great deal of electricity for each kilogram of hydrogen, and making enough for steelmaking demands huge amounts of cheap renewable power, which is the main cost and scale barrier.
A photon's energy is tied to its wavelength, and pushing the frequency higher keeps shrinking that wavelength toward nothing, so the energy each photon carries collapses toward zero along with it.

A photon's energy equals Planck's constant multiplied by its frequency, so raising the frequency raises the energy in direct proportion, which is why ultraviolet photons carry more energy than red ones.
For small swings the period is two pi times the square root of length over gravitational acceleration, so a longer pendulum swings more slowly, and nothing else about the pendulum enters the formula.
The string's material sets how much it stretches under the bob's weight, and a stretchier string changes the effective length of the swing, so what the string is made of shifts the period.
In the core, four hydrogen nuclei are joined step by step into a single helium nucleus, and the small mass lost in combining them is released as the energy that makes the star shine.
Turning hydrogen into helium involves nuclei being broken apart and rearranged, with protons converting into neutrons along the way, so the star's energy comes from nuclei splitting and reassembling.
One connection stays open the whole session to carry commands and replies, while a fresh connection opens for each file transfer, so commands can still be sent while bulk data is moving.
Files sent across a network need protecting in transit, so one channel scrambles the outgoing data and the other unscrambles it at the receiving end, keeping the two security jobs apart.
A wave advances one full wavelength in each cycle, and the number of cycles per second is the frequency, so the distance covered each second is the wavelength multiplied by the frequency.
Frequency counts cycles per second and wavelength is the length of each cycle, so dividing how often the wave repeats by how long each repeat is gives how fast the wave travels.
The relativistic mass is the rest mass multiplied by the Lorentz factor, and that factor grows without limit as the speed nears that of light, which is why no finite energy can get the object there.
Only massless particles like photons can travel at light speed, so an object pushed closer and closer to that speed must be shedding mass along the way until nothing remains at the limit.

Entangled particles each carry their own clock, and relativity says those clocks run at different rates depending on motion, so the linked measurements expose the strange slowing of time between the two particles.

Measuring one entangled particle instantly fixes correlated results for its partner however far away it is, and Bell test violations show no local hidden cause explains that, which clashes with locality in spacetime.

At high temperature molecules move fast enough that their attractions hardly matter, and at high pressure they are pushed into steady, uniform collisions, so both conditions make the gas follow the simple ideal law.

Low pressure spreads the molecules far apart so their own volume is negligible, and high temperature gives them enough kinetic energy that intermolecular attractions barely matter, which matches the ideal gas assumptions.

Earth's tilted spin axis makes each hemisphere lean toward the Sun for part of the year, giving it more direct sunlight and longer days, which is why the hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.

The Sun's output rises and falls with its bursts of activity, and those swings change how much energy reaches Earth over the year, so the warm and cold seasons follow the Sun's active and quiet periods.
A red giant's outer envelope is cool and very opaque, so radiation cannot carry the energy through efficiently, and large rising and sinking currents of gas take over the job of moving heat outward.

A red giant's outer layers are extremely thin and spread out, so energy works its way outward through the slow random wandering of particles and photons, gradually spreading through the diffuse envelope.

The field equations of general relativity contain a gravitomagnetic part, so moving masses produce effects much like magnetism, and the theory treats gravity as a field built on the pattern of electromagnetism.

In the theory, mass and energy bend the geometry around them, and objects in free fall simply follow the straightest possible paths through that bent geometry, which we experience as gravitational attraction.
Wien's law makes the peak wavelength inversely proportional to temperature, so a hotter body peaks at shorter wavelengths, which is why the hottest stars look bluish while cooler ones look red.
A hotter body glows more intensely and gives off more energy overall, and as heated metal goes from dull to bright red, the glow moves toward the longer, redder end of the spectrum.
Polaris is found by following the two pointer stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl, and the Dipper is part of the Great Bear, so the North Star belongs to that same bear figure.
Polaris sits at the end of the handle of the Little Dipper, and the Little Dipper is the main pattern of the Little Bear, so the North Star belongs to the smaller of the two bears.
Quarks inside protons and neutrons are held together by exchanging massless particles that carry color charge, and the residual of that exchange is what binds nucleons in the nucleus as well.
The nuclear forces act inside the nucleus over very short ranges, which requires a heavy carrier particle, and the charged heavy boson that changes protons into neutrons is the one acting there.
Current flowing into a junction has to be accounted for by the law relating magnetic fields to the currents that pass through a closed loop, which keeps track of all the current crossing a boundary.

Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so whatever charge flows in each second must flow out, and the junction rule of circuit analysis states exactly that the incoming currents equal the outgoing ones.
Light entering glass is absorbed and re-emitted by the atoms in the material, and that process breaks up the original wave, so the incoming wavelength no longer exists as such inside the glass.

The frequency stays fixed at the boundary while light slows down in glass, and since wavelength equals speed divided by frequency, the slower speed gives a correspondingly shorter wavelength inside the glass.
The second element was made in huge amounts in the Big Bang and is constantly produced in every star's core, so it builds up across the whole universe as the main product of all that stellar fusion.
The Big Bang produced mostly the simplest element, a single proton with one electron, and it still makes up the large majority of all ordinary matter by mass, far ahead of anything else.
The particles of a medium are always jostling with thermal motion, and the wave adds only a small disturbance on top of that, so their movement relative to the wave's travel has no fixed direction.
On a rope shaken up and down, each piece of rope moves up and down while the wave pulse travels along its length, so the motion of the medium is at right angles to the wave's travel.

The limit marks the point where a star's internal thermal pressure becomes equal to the pressure of its gas, so beyond that luminosity the extra heat cannot be supported by the gas and the balance breaks.
At that luminosity the outward push of photons scattering off electrons exactly matches the inward gravitational pull on the gas, so any brighter object would start blowing its own outer layers away.
A tether hanging tens of thousands of kilometers must support its own weight, so the material's strength relative to its density sets the longest cable that can hang without snapping under itself.

A tether stretching from the ground into space passes through huge temperature swings between sunlight and shadow, and the resulting expansion and contraction strains the cable, limiting how long it can safely be.
This ice giant has a set of narrow, dark rings that extend far around the planet, and because they encircle it on its sideways tilt they cover a wider region than the rings of any other planet.
The second-largest planet has broad, bright rings of ice that span hundreds of thousands of kilometers and are visible through a small telescope, far larger than the faint rings of the other giants.

The Milky Way and its neighbours are all being pulled toward this concentration of mass, and the gravitationally bound group of galaxies we live in is what moves with it, so it is our local grouping itself.

It is a gravitational anomaly tens of megaparsecs away that pulls on many galaxy clusters at once, and a mass that large spanning several clusters is the scale of a structure built from clusters themselves.

Solving the Friedmann equation with matter density falling as the inverse cube of the scale factor gives a scale factor proportional to time raised to two thirds, the classic Einstein-de Sitter result.
Matter pulls on itself and adds energy that drives the expansion, so with density feeding the growth rate, the scale factor picks up speed and goes as the square of time.
A neutron star is extraordinarily hot and bright when it forms, and the outward push of all that intense radiation is what holds its matter up against the inward pull of its own gravity.
Neutrons are fermions, so the exclusion principle forbids them from sharing quantum states, and when packed tightly that resistance to compression supports the star until the mass gets too large.
When food stretches the stomach and proteins arrive, cells in the stomach's lower region release a hormone that drives both acid secretion and stronger contractions, moving the meal along.
After a meal the body has to mobilize stored energy to power digestion, and the pancreatic hormone that raises blood sugar also speeds the stomach's churning so the meal gets processed faster.
Current rockets are too slow to reach distant destinations quickly, so trips beyond Earth orbit stretch over months or years, and the lack of faster engines is what caps how long crews can be out.

Past the shelter of Earth's magnetic field, crews absorb cosmic and solar radiation steadily, and every extra month needs more food, water and air carried at great launch cost, so both limit mission length.

In the cycle the heavier nuclei act only as catalysts and are regenerated at the end, while four protons are consumed and fused into one helium nucleus, so the fuel actually used up is the lightest element.
The cycle begins when a proton is captured by a nucleus with six protons, and without that seed nothing in the sequence can start, so the element that opens the cycle is what it runs on.

Long-period comets arrive from every direction, which points to a vast spherical shell of icy bodies far beyond the planets, proposed to explain them and never directly observed, so it remains hypothetical.
The solar system is ringed by a band of countless small bodies orbiting the Sun, and that collection of fragments, many holding water ice, is the cloud of objects that surrounds the inner planets.
Producing eggs costs a reptile a great deal of stored energy, so ovulation is triggered once the female has eaten enough to build up reserves, and a good food supply is the signal to reproduce.
In induced ovulators the egg is released in response to mating itself rather than an internal cycle, so the physical stimulus of a male mounting is what sets ovulation off in those species.

Setting kinetic energy equal to the gravitational binding energy gives escape velocity as the square root of two G times the planet's mass over its radius, so only those two planetary quantities appear.
A planet's magnetic field traps and holds charged particles, adding to the grip of its mass, so escaping requires overcoming both the gravitational pull and the magnetic hold of the planet together.
A bird's flight speed comes from how hard it flaps and how much power its muscles deliver, while wing loading only describes weight spread over wing area, so it shapes manoeuvring but not speed.
A bird with more weight on each unit of wing area needs more airflow to generate enough lift, so its minimum and cruising speeds both rise, which is why heavily loaded wings go with faster flight.
The ring's dust is too sparse to reflect much sunlight, but it is warm compared with deep space and glows at long wavelengths, so a space telescope sensing that thermal emission picked it up.

Sparse dust and gas around Saturn absorb and scatter ultraviolet light in distinctive patterns, so splitting that light into its spectrum reveals faint material that cannot be picked out in ordinary images.
The limit is the mass above which electron degeneracy pressure can no longer hold up a remnant, and the remnant supported by electron degeneracy is the small dense one left by Sun-like stars.
The limit sets the heaviest star that can stay small and cool while still supported, and the small, dim, cool stars at the bottom of the main sequence are exactly the ones sitting under that ceiling.
